# On Writing Without a Reason

There's something strange about being told to fill a quota with nothing else to guide you. No prompt to answer, no problem to solve, no audience to please—just a number to reach and a blank space to reach it in. It's a little like being handed a shovel and told to dig, except no one's told you where, or why, or what you're supposed to find.

So I'll start with the obvious: most writing exists to do something. Persuade, inform, entertain, confess. Even bad writing usually has a job, however poorly executed. But writing without a job is a different animal. It's closer to thinking out loud, except thinking out loud usually has the decency to trail off when it gets boring. Words on a page don't get that luxury. They have to keep coming, one after another, whether or not they're earning their place.

I think about how children draw when you give them a piece of paper and nothing else. They don't ask what to draw. They just start, and shapes accumulate, and eventually something resembling a house or a dog or a sun with too many rays emerges, not because they planned it but because the act of drawing produces its own direction. Maybe writing works the same way. You put down a word, and that word suggests the next one, and before long you're somewhere you didn't intend to be, which might be the only interesting place to end up.

There's a temptation, when given total freedom, to write about freedom itself—to make the blank page the subject of the blank page. It's a bit recursive, a bit cheap, like a magician explaining that the trick is that there is no trick. But maybe that's fine. Maybe the honest response to an open assignment is to admit that openness is disorienting, that infinite possibility doesn't feel like freedom so much as a mild vertigo. Tell someone they can write about anything and watch how often they freeze. Constraints are scaffolding. Take them away and you discover how much you depended on walls to know which direction was up.

So here is a confession: I don't know what I'm building. I started this without an image in mind, the way you might start walking without a destination, just to see what's a few blocks over. Sometimes that's how the best discoveries happen—not through aimed effort but through wandering that happens to pass by something interesting. Penicillin was an accident. So was the microwave oven, depending on which story you believe, when a chocolate bar melted in someone's pocket near a magnetron. Serendipity has a way of rewarding people who are simply moving, even without a map.

But I don't want to oversell the romance of aimlessness. Most wandering doesn't lead anywhere except back to where you started, tired and unenlightened. For every accidental discovery there are a thousand walks that just end in walks. The truth is probably duller than the myth: most of what you find by wandering is more wandering. The value isn't necessarily in arriving somewhere but in the wandering having happened at all—in the muscles that get exercised, in the attention that gets paid to things you'd otherwise walk past.

This essay, if it can be called that, is closer to a muscle exercise than a destination. Words are being put down, sentences are accumulating, and somewhere in the accumulation a kind of momentum builds that wouldn't exist if I'd stopped to ask whether each sentence deserved to exist. There's a lesson in that, maybe, about the difference between editing and generating. They're different muscles, different mental postures. The generator just needs to keep moving. The editor comes later, with a colder eye, asking what's worth keeping. Right now I'm only the generator. The editor isn't invited yet.

It strikes me that this is true of a lot of human effort, not just writing. We separate the doing from the judging, sometimes without realizing it. People who write a little every day, badly, often outpace people who wait for inspiration to write something brilliant on the first try. The waiting is its own trap. It dresses itself up as standards, as taste, as not wanting to waste time on something mediocre, but really it's often just fear wearing a nicer coat. Generate first. Judge later. The order matters more than people admit.

I notice I've drifted from talking about writing into something like advice, which wasn't the plan, except there was no plan, so I suppose it can't have drifted from anything. That's the strange permission of this kind of writing—nothing is off-topic because there was no topic to begin with. It's the closest thing to free association that still resembles prose. A diary entry without a self to confess. A speech without an audience to convince.

Maybe that's the real subject here: what happens to language when you strip away its usual obligations. It doesn't collapse. It doesn't run dry. It just becomes a little more honest about what it's doing, which is filling space, making patterns, accumulating until accumulation itself starts to feel like a kind of meaning. Not the meaning of statement or argument, but the meaning of motion—the sense that something happened here, words were arranged, attention was spent, and somewhere in that spending, however small, something was made that wasn't here before.

That's not nothing. It might not be much. But it's not nothing.
